If youâve seen The Pitt, youâve got an idea of what happens behind the scenes in an emergency vet hospital. Thereâs always another case to see, another owner to talk to, another patient to check up on. The biggest difference is that we donât often refer things. The initial emergency clinician is also the one assessing the radiographs, interpreting bloodwork, performing surgeries, and managing hospitalized cases. Itâs not uncommon for me to have a critical ICU patient Iâm managing at the same time as Iâm working up an ear infection, or about to go into surgery for a C-section.

Anyone who walks through the ER doors gets triaged, and I see what I can. This can be ear infections, severe dog bite wounds, or behavioral issues.

The most rewarding part of working in emergency veterinary medicine? When the patient is feeling good enough to try to bite you!

Initially, I wasnât sure if I wanted to go to veterinary school. I worked in a boarding clinic attached to a general practice that occasionally let me help on the medicine side, but I wasnât sold on vet med. I didnât get into veterinary school my first application round, so I found a job at a local emergency clinic. My working interview was so wild, I realized Iâd found my passion!

Emergencies come in waves! Some days are âDiarrhea Day,â where everything that comes in has diarrhea. I had âUrine Dayâ last week! By far, Iâd say GI upsets (vomiting, diarrhea, not eating) are the most common ER cases.

Seizures, protracted vomiting, severe weakness. I think anything that comes on suddenly should be investigated quickly!

If youâre worried, Iâm worried. You know your pet best, and if you feel something is âoffâ â donât wait! Even if itâs just for an exam or to get vitals, itâs well worth the peace of mind.

Itâs totally okay to be open about your budget and what you can and cannot do. The ER tends to be more expensive than a daytime practice, and we acknowledge that.  Our job is not to judge; itâs to help! If that means stabilizing until your vet can see you in a few hours, letâs do that.

I saw a lot of disinformation online. I figured if I was louder, I could drown out the bad advice.

I try to time my posts with real-world presentations. Heat stroke cases in the summer, toxicities around the holidays. Sometimes I just have a really interesting case, and I share it right then and there.

That veterinarians are humans too! I post a lot of information for other veterinary professionals, and I hope pet owners see the comments and realize how engaged the community is. Here is a group of people talking about vet med on their day off, learning about cases and new studies, and trying to keep up to date on the latest medicine.

Veterinary medicine is very science-focused. While we are always learning, thereâs a sort of structure to it that doesnât allow for much movement. My books are a whole different part of my brain, one where I can be creative and silly and make up worlds!

âAnother Damn Rescueâ is a spicy shifter romcom where a veterinarian finds an injured âdogâ on the side of the road, only to realize heâs a wolf shifter. Itâs ultimately a love letter to vet med, where I talk about the struggles we face, while also showing the humor and humanity. Oh, and how amazing veterinary technicians, assistants, and receptionists are!

Itâs more of a good time, kick your feet up and giggle sort of story! Pet owners might gain some insight into what itâs like to work in vet med in 2026. Veterinary professionals will enjoy seeing themselves accurately represented in media with a happy ever after!

The podcast is an extension of my social media â itâs a resource for other vets when theyâre not sure where to go. Itâs mostly focused on education for other veterinarians. I bring on specialists and let them pick a topic they feel passionate about. Think of it as continuing education.

Bridging my author identity with my veterinary one is very scary, but also very cool! Iâm especially excited about the podcast because I hope to get companies to talk about new products before they launch as well.

Fatigue! Thereâs compassion and ethical fatigue, where we feel helpless in the face of obstacles outside our reach. Some days I think, âI didnât help anyone today.â And thatâs not true; itâs the story we tell ourselves when weâre in that headspace.

Sometimes we need to take a step back and remember that this is that person's worst day. Ultimately, the team is there to help you. While we donât tolerate abuse, we TOTALLY UNDERSTAND being upset, overwhelmed, having decision paralysis, and everything else that goes along with these scary situations!

I am a pet owner as well as a veterinarian, and Iâve had cases that hit me as a pet owner as well. âIâve been in your shoes before,â goes a long way for owners in these situations. Weâre often told not to interject our opinions, but I am quick to tell owners that Iâve had a pet in the same situation.

Keep ALL of your records! Ask your vet to email you bloodworkand keep it in a folder. Take pictures of your pet's medications. Walking into the ER and saying âHereâs Fluffyâs last bloodworkâ and âhereâs the medication Fluffy is onâ is SO valuable!

XYLITOL!! It can cause fatal low blood sugar and liver damage. Itâs in sugar-free gum, and lately theyâve been calling it âbirch sugar,â so not a lot of people realize itâs the same thing.

Good mentorship is worth its weight in gold! Even the best veterinary school on the planet will not prepare you to step right into an ER without assistance. Ask for help, and find people who are willing to help you learn.

The clock is ticking, but there's still hope for a festive flower show. Choosing the right bulbs and growing conditions can make all the difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s not necessarily too late to plant amaryllis bulbs for Christmas, but timing does matter. Amaryllis typically blooms six to eight weeks after planting, so early to mid-November is your last chance to get bulbs in the pot if you want striking holiday flowers in time for the big day.

If you’re growing amaryllis for holiday flowers, choose the right type. Amaryllis usually refers to Hippeastrum, a South American native, not true Amaryllis, also known as belladonna lilies from South Africa. Most Hippeastrum bulbs sold this time of year are grown in the Southern Hemisphere and will bloom in six to eight weeks. Dutch-grown bulbs take longer, so avoid these.

Flowering also varies by the plant’s growing conditions, which means you have some control. While early or mid-November is the ideal time to plant a holiday amaryllis, you can do a few things to speed up the process if you’ve just missed the window.

Getting healthy holiday blooms isn’t just luck. How you choose and plant your bulbs is important. Start by selecting the best bulbs. Look for large, firm, and healthy bulbs without soft spots, damage, or mold. If you see a bulb that has the tip of a green stem emerging, grab it. This bulb has already begun to break dormancy and should flower sooner.

While unusual varieties can be expensive, you don't need to spend a lot of money on bulbs – Walmart sells preplanted bulbs for under $6.

Next, choose a good-quality potting mix, such as Miracle-Gro Indoor Potting Mix, available at Amazon, and a container with drainage holes that is only one or two inches (2.5 to 5 cm) wider than the bulb. Position the bulb in the pot so that the pointy end is up and one-third to one-half of the bulb is above the surface of the potting mix.

Water your planted bulb thoroughly, letting it all drain through, before setting it in a warm, bright spot. Keep the potting mix just slightly damp, never soggy. Amaryllis doesn’t need much water and can rot in soggy conditions.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While you can’t significantly alter the timeline for flowering, a few easy tips encourage strong and steady growth:

You can’t do a lot to force it, but these conditions provide everything your plant needs for a healthy growth rate. Just don’t overdo it. Fertilizer, too much heat, and too much water can do more harm than good.

Be realistic about timing with amaryllis bulbs. If it’s late November, you might still have time for a Christmas flower. Choose the largest, healthiest bulb, with a bit of green growth, if possible, for the best start. Provide the best conditions and cross your fingers.

If it’s already December, you won’t get a flower by Christmas from a dormant bulb. However, you can probably find a potted amaryllis that has already broken dormancy and has a stem. This plant will likely bloom by Christmas.

You got some gorgeous blooms in time for Christmas, but now you want them to last. It’s time to switch your care strategy from encouraging growth to keeping flowers looking their best.

When the flowers do fade, snip them off to keep the plant looking tidy. Once all the flowers are done blooming, cut the stem back close to the bulb. With the right care, you should enjoy healthy, attractive flowers for two to three weeks.

Here are a few great options available to buy now, with beautiful blooms that will bring a festive splash of color to your home.

Whether you get flowers in time for Christmas or not, forcing an amaryllis bulb indoors is a great winter activity. Enjoy your blooms, even if they don’t open until January. And if you’re up for it, you can keep the plant going and encourage it to bloom again next year.

#7974. Wise Words from Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas as to Access to Court Records

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

My Stanford law school colleagues Nora and David Engstrom, as well as Berkeley law professor Jonah Gelbach and others, have asked the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules recommend a new Rule of Civil Procedure (5.3) governing the sealing of court records. I think this is an excellent idea: While there is a good deal of precedent on the question, distilling it into a rule that can easily be consulted by judges, lawyers, law clerks, and pro se litigants would be very helpful.

Just today, Third Circuit Judge Stephanos Bibas (also a former law professor), submitted a letter endorsing the proposed rule, and I thought it was much worth passing along:

Dear Members of the Advisory Committee on Civil Rules:

I write to express my strong support for proposed Rule 5.3, a much-needed recapitulation of the procedural standards governing sealing of judicial records.

The public has a presumptive right to access judicial records. This right serves several important societal functions. By exposing the records of private wrongdoing to the public eye, this right deters further wrongdoing. By forcing the government to litigate out in the open, it empowers the public "to keep a watchful eye on the workings of public agencies." Nixon v. Warner Commc'ns, Inc., 435 U.S. 589, 598 (1978). And by enabling the public to dig into the bases for judicial decisions, it enables the public to assure itself of the strength of judicial reasoning, the cornerstone of judicial legitimacy. This right thus not only "diminishes possibilities for injustice, incompetence, perjury, and fraud," but also provides "the public with a more complete understanding of the judicial system and a better perception of its fairness." In re Avandia Mktg., Sales Prac. & Prod. Liab. Litig., 924 F.3d 662, 672 (3d Cir. 2019) (internal quotation marks omitted).

On paper, this right looks strong. In the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where I sit, a district court issuing an order to seal "must articulate the compelling, countervailing interests to be protected" and "make specific findings on the record concerning the effects of disclosure." Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). But that standard is a paper tiger—mighty in appearance, but toothless in practice. Time and again, we see cases on appeal where the parties asked to seal large parts of the record below, and the district court, with little discussion, agreed to do so.

Take one recent motion to seal in a Third Circuit case. The district court had certified a multi-state class action against a car company. On appeal, the company asked us to seal ten volumes of appendices, totaling nearly three thousand pages of material. The company told us that sealing was necessary to prevent competitors from copying its design choices, stealing its engineering solutions, and exploiting its sales strategy.

But it took only a cursory glance at the appendices to see how overbroad the company's request was. Hundreds of pages, for example, covered deposition testimony from one of the plaintiff's lay witnesses, a mechanic who had worked on the defendant's cars and had commented on their alleged defects. Hundreds of other pages dealt with one of the plaintiffs' experts, who had opined on the veracity of the defendant's public comments and sales catalogues. But if the mechanic based his testimony on his day-to-day work on the defendant's cars, and the expert had based his testimony on the company's public statements, how would these materials reveal competitive secrets? So I denied the request without prejudice, asking the company to come back with a narrower request if it so chose. But why had the record below been sealed in the first place?

It should come as little surprise that motions to seal almost always go unopposed. The harm of overbroad sealing falls on future victims of repeat tortfeasors, future litigants in related cases, and the public at large. It does not fall on the parties to the case.

Indeed, the parties generally have an active interest in secrecy. The party who moves to seal records fears that the information produced in the case could lead to bad press coverage, competitive harms, or even follow-on litigation. The other party presumably does not share those same concerns about broad disclosure, but it does not share the public's concerns about overbroad sealing, either.

So in the give-and-take game of litigation, where it can be important to reserve your capital for fighting the fights that matter to your client, opposing a motion to seal is a waste of that capital. At the very least, it is a waste of time and money. For lawyers in an active dispute—so used to viewing themselves as only agents of their clients, and not also officers of the court—submitting an opposition to an overbroad motion to seal might not seem worth the cost of the paper to print it.

This leaves it to district-court judges to police these motions and protect the public's presumptive right of access to judicial records. But what my experience as a judge on the court of appeals has taught me, Professor Engstrom et. al's empirical work now confirms: Most district courts rubber-stamp these requests.

This might come as a surprise to some members of the Judicial Conference. After all, the law of every circuit requires district courts to reject requests to seal that are too broad to be justified by their supposed rationale.

So why do district courts frequently fail to apply that law? One problem might be the lack of developed precedent in this area. Because motions to seal are almost never subject to full treatment in district court opinions, let alone appellate review, there are few decisions applying legal standards to specific facts, teasing out what interests suffice to justify sealing, and how broad is too broad. Without clearly factually analogous precedent to rely on, district courts might be more hesitant to deny a motion to seal as overbroad, even though the operative legal standard compels that result.

Another problem is rooted in the lack of adversarial presentation. With no one on the other side, inflated claims of confidentiality go unchallenged.

Other problems might boil down to the mechanics of busy district court dockets. Perhaps, for example, when a district court grants a protective order, that decision generates an inertial force that skews the outcome of the subsequent motion to seal, even though the two decisions are subject to different legal standards. Or perhaps a motion to seal, because it is unopposed, slips under the radar, resembling an administrative matter to be rubber-stamped rather than a legal decision to be carefully scrutinized.

But whatever the reason, the results are clear: For most motions to seal, "the parties agree, the busy district court accommodates, and nobody is left in the courtroom to question whether the decision satisfied the substantive requirements." Binh Hoa Le v. Exeter Fin. Corp., 990 F.3d 410, 417 (5th Cir. 2021).

This proposed rule will push parties and courts alike to do better. First, this proposed rule will ensure that the parties know what their obligations are when they submit a motion to seal. I often sit by designation on the District of Delaware, where I regularly receive motions to seal with no accompanying explanation or justification, putting the onus on me to push the parties for more. Under Proposed Rule 5.3(c), parties will be reminded that, as our circuit has regularly held, "[b]road allegations of harm, bereft of specific examples or articulated reasoning, are insufficient." In re Avandia Mktg., 924 F.3d at 673 (internal quotation marks omitted).

Second, this proposed rule will act as a process-forcing mechanism for busy district court judges. District courts lack the benefit of adversarial litigation over motions to seal. And without a party opposing a motion, it is easy to think that no reasoning is needed for an order—if no party loses, the thinking goes, no party needs a basis for the court's decision.

Proposed Rule 5.3(h) makes clear that even without an adversarial party, the district court must act as the steward of the public interest in accessing court records, and must reason through its decision. The decision to seal is for the court to make by applying the correct legal standard, not for the parties to make by means of consent. Proposed Rule 5.3(i) provides a checklist that a district court can use in reaching that decision.

Finally, the proposed rule will remind parties and district courts alike that sealing is not an all-or-nothing question. Proposed Rule 5.3(d)(3) and (g) make clear that, where viable, the default approach should be targeted redactions. The choice is not between disclosing a list of social security numbers and sealing an entire document. A happy medium is often readily available.

This proposed rule does not make new law. Sunlight is the best disinfectant for many societal ills, yet sealing "insulates the participants" in the legal process, "masking impropriety, obscuring incompetence, and concealing corruption." Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. v. F.T.C., 710 F.2d 1165, 1179 (6th Cir. 1983). Judicial reasoning is the basis for judicial legitimacy, yet sealing "withdraws an element of the judicial process from public view," making "the ensuing decision look more like fiat." Matter of Krynicki, 983 F.2d 74, 75 (7th Cir. 1992) (Easterbrook, J.). For these reasons, the courts of appeals have consistently held that the public has a presumptive right to access judicial records, one that should only be abrogated where necessary, and even there only to the extent necessary. This proposed rule simply makes that right harder to neglect.

My then-student Jennifer Welson and I had unsuccessfully proposed a sealing rule to the Rule Committee in 2020, on behalf of the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and Electronic Frontier Foundation; but I much hope that the Engstrom et al. proposal, which is backed by considerably more empirical research than mine had been, will be more successful.

NEXT: From a Life-Long Republican Contemplating the Election Results

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Kate Hudson’s silver, bronze, and gold bow tree is a nostalgic Christmas look. Experts share how to get it right without it feeling dated.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's official; Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree from last year is still inspiring holiday decorations in 2026.

It's hardly a surprise. After all, the actress (best known for her starring turns in Bride Wars and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days) kept her Christmas tree simple, classy, and very less is more: think silver, bronze and gold bows, a few ornaments and not much else.

Now, a bow is almost as Christmassy as it gets, whether it’s tied on a tree, a wreath or a present. A nostalgic tree does have one risk, though: if you do it without thinking it through, it can go from warm and charming to dated really quickly. Some experts gave me tips on how you can avoid this, and get Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree look.

For those who have yet to see Kate Hudson's Christmas tree in all its glory, flick your eyes downwards...

A post shared by Kate Hudson (@katehudson)

It feels like a rebellion against the minimalist matchy-matchy (and beige) trend that has been going on for so many years, doesn't it? “People are tired of the same old, store-bought, themed trees,” says Irena Cara, interior designer and co-founder of Nova Wrap.

Reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, points to Millennial parents whose kids are now the age they were in the 1990s. Many of them, he says, want to revive “the warm, festive and childlike vibe of a 90s Christmas, as opposed to what people are now calling the ‘sad beige’ of contemporary tree styling.”

So, how best to recreate it? Other than buying some of this beautiful metallic gold ribbon from Amazon. We have a few ideas...

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Hey, we might not have Goldie Hawn as a mum, but when it comes to Christmas nostalgia, a lot of millennials remember our parents' houses being packed with all kinds of stuff, and so much color that it felt cluttered. So, the biggest worry with going with a nostalgic look is the tree looking tacky.

For Renwick, “the biggest challenge for anyone trying to create a nostalgic tree is how to evade the ‘tacky’ accusations.” His answer is to look at what Kate Hudson did with hers. “The whole point of this ‘comeback’ thing is to evoke the festive vibe of the 90s, not to recreate it in painstaking detail,” he says.

Shop Nostalgic Christmas Tree Essentials:

Want the Kate Hudson look? “My advice is to use the metallic bows with restraint, in such a way that they stand out but still leave space for the other decorations and the tree itself to still be visible,” says Renwick.

Cara has practical tips for gold, silver, and bronze. “Use brushed or matte ribbon to take the ‘shiny’ edge off, especially if the metals are varying warm tones. Also, make sure the bows are of varying sizes, to keep things interesting.”

For quantity, she says: “On a tree between 6 and 7 feet, use between 20 and 30 bows.” Lighting matters too: “Warm white lights make metallics look even better.”

A Christmas tree runs the risk of feeling tacky, true, but it can also feel too generic, like it should be in a department store in the 90s. Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a way to avoid this.

“You can’t purchase nostalgia, but you can tie it!” she says. Her suggestion is to reuse ribbon that already means something. “Use ribbons that have a story, such as paper that a bouquet you received came wrapped in. On the loose end of the ribbon, write down the date you received it, and now your tree is a timeline.”

Melam preserves flowers for a living, so she also suggests pairing a ribbon with a flower from your own garden. She says you can build the look slowly: “You can add one more ribbon to your tree each year.”

If you already have tons of ornaments that have been passed down by family or maybe something your kids have made, bows can tie them into a whole scheme.

Cara says to put the old pieces where people look first: “Place heirloom and vintage pieces at eye level in the center where people look first.” Then, let the ribbon link everything together. “Match the ribbon to details on the older ornaments, such as a gold edge or a red glass.”

A big advantage of a bow tree like Kate Hudson's is that it’s very cheap to update, as ribbon is super easy to swap out for different colors and patterns. “Swap out the ribbon and keep the ornaments to change decorations year to year for a small cost,” says Cara.

Melam says to store ribbon carefully between seasons: “Moisture and light will cause your ribbon to fade, so store it flat in a cool, dark, dry place.”

Kate Hudson’s tree works because it feels warm and traditional without trying to look like a time capsule. Keep your color palette tight and give your ribbon some history to recreate the same nostalgia.

She also writes about the latest gardening news and emerging trends, from pollinator-friendly planting to small-space edible gardens and sustainable outdoor living. When she’s not covering a viral moment, she’s cultivating her own love of gardening and bringing a storyteller’s eye to all things green and growing.

An employee of OpenAI has been arrested for and charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a national of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, was arrested on Oct. 9, and made his initial appearance in federal court today.

“This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump’s leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important,” said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. “I thank Director Patel and our FBI partners for their diligence and swift action. The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America’s cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats.”

“According to the complaint unsealed today, Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer’s executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting American SI innovation is essential to safeguarding our nation’s economic strength and national security, and the FBI views that mission as one of our highest counterintelligence priorities. Thank you to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and our law enforcement partners for their support — and we will continue working closely with our partners across the U.S. government and private sector to keep American businesses and citizens safe and to ensure our country maintains its competitive edge.”

“The Bay Area and Silicon Valley lead the world in developing tomorrow’s technology, and our Office will continue to stand at the forefront of protecting that American innovation,” said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian for the Northern District of California. “For us it is a matter of national security. This arrest highlights our relentless efforts in partnership with the FBI to identify and prosecute those who seek to steal our technology, as alleged in the complaint.”

According to the complaint, Alfozan had been employed as an engineer by OpenAI since July 2025. On or about Sept. 30, OpenAI personnel discovered a surreptitious audio recording device (Recording Device 1) inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room inside one of their buildings in San Francisco. OpenAI determined that the device, which had been concealed in toilet paper, was installed on or about Sept. 28, and that its contents were encrypted.

Closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage inside OpenAI’s office showed that Alfozan appeared near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery, although he had no authority to access or to participate in meetings occurring in the executive conference room. According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about Open AI’s technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships.

According to the complaint, prior to Sept. 28, Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about Open AI’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, “leadership and exec” locations, and external partner meetings. Moreover, a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse (which shared multiple identifiers and attributes with Alfozan’s own chatbot account) submitted prompts between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 related to building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device, including inquiries about “build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,” “customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,” “improv[ing] audio and live listening,” and “encrypt[ing] the SD card,” among other things. The same chatbot account also submitted prompts specifically related to Recording Device 1, including its custom header and unique MAC address, between Sept. 27 and Sept. 28.

The complaint further alleges that on Oct. 5, Alfozan entered the executive conference room and appeared to look behind the television into which Recording Device 1 had been inserted, as captured below:

Finally, the complaint alleges that, also on or about Oct. 5, Alfozan left a bag unattended in a different room in an OpenAI building. OpenAI security personnel found and opened Alfozan’s bag, inside which they discovered — among other things, including Alfozan’s wallet and ID — another recording device (Recording Device 2) similar to Recording Device 1.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of 5 years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by 3 years of supervised release.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Parker for the Northern District of California is prosecuting the case with valuable assistance from Trial Attorney Kate Tagert of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section.

This prosecution is in support of National Security Presidential Memorandum 11 (NSPM-11) designed to support American superiority in super intelligence technology.

#7969. Fifth Circuit on Pseudonymity of Libel Defendant (Who Claims She Was Sexually Assaulted)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Doe v. Roe, decided today by Fifth Circuit Judges Jennifer Walker Elrod, Carolyn Dineen King, and Carl Stewart:

After receiving notice of Jane Roe's impending California lawsuit involving allegations of sexual assault and sexual harassment, John Doe sued Roe in the Southern District of Mississippi, alleging that Roe was attempting to extort and defame him. Roe moved to proceed pseudonymously in the Mississippi lawsuit. The district court denied her permission to do so. Roe appeals that decision, raising several concerns with the district court's analysis. Because we agree with some of Roe's arguments, we vacate and remand for the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously….

Roe argues that allegations of sexual assault involve matters of the utmost intimacy [and can thus justify pseudonymity]. We agree. There is no doubt that requiring alleged rape and sexual assault victims to proceed "under their real identities would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." It is no surprise, then, that numerous courts have allowed alleged victims of sexual misconduct to proceed under a pseudonym, "including when they are defendants being sued for libel and related torts."

We agree with Roe. To start, we are not persuaded that the proverbial cat is out of the bag here. True, publicly available information cannot be obscured by courts. However, that internet sleuths might speculate that Roe is a particular person because her California complaint "lines up with [her] public profile" is not the same as a public broadcasting of Roe's certain identity. As to the fact that Roe's name was a matter of public record for short periods, that was either because of Doe's actions (which Roe objected to), or Roe's inadvertent disclosures which counsel corrected and constituted no waiver (which we address below)….

Last, Roe argues that she did not waive her right to proceed anonymously. Again, we agree. Roe never waived her ability to request pseudonymity because her conduct does not constitute an "intentional relinquishment" of that position. Roe's opposition to Doe's motion to proceed pseudonymously waived nothing because Roe's position was that she should be allowed to proceed pseudonymously while he should not be. And any confusion about Roe's position based on the precise language in her opposition brief was clarified by her own subsequent motions seeking to seal or redact Doe's amended complaint (which used Roe's real name) and to proceed pseudonymously.

Further, Doe's use of Roe's real name in open court did not constitute waiver on Roe's behalf because, at the time, Doe had already publicly named Roe in his amended complaint, Roe had a pending motion seeking to seal or redact that amended complaint naming her, and Roe objected to the use of her name at the hearing (even if not as fast as a prudent attorney likely should have). Finally, we are not convinced that Roe's inadvertent disclosures of her real name in the California case and on this appeal constitute waiver. The disclosures were unintentional, were made in portions of larger filings, and Roe took steps to correct the errors once becoming aware of them, resulting in the sealing and refiling of the documents. These facts do not demonstrate that Roe intentionally relinquished her request to proceed pseudonymously….

In light of the clarifications provided in this opinion, we find that it is appropriate to allow the district court to reconsider whether Roe should be permitted to proceed under a pseudonym in this case. {We acknowledge Doe's argument that allowing Roe to proceed under a pseudonym would be prejudicial to him. We think that argument is best left for the district court to address in the first instance on remand.}

All-year backyard structure on a budget? Yes please! Evergreen shrubs are the landscape-design must every garden is missing, and these can all be planted now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As leaves drop in fall, I always wish I’d planted more evergreen shrubs in my garden to give structure and color all through the winter. From tall arborvitae cones to slender columns of holly and perfect no-prune spheres, evergreens give a garden a shapely skeleton on which to hang seasonal blooms. While I’m lucky enough to have mature yew hedges and an old conifer I’m planning to cloud-prune, I want to add evergreen accents to borders and alongside a path to punctuate my garden design. Globes of green leaves in patio planters are high on my wish list too.

What's stopped me? One of the basic principles of garden design is to always repeat-plant evergreens in odd numbers – and bying multiple plants gets expensive, fast. But Home Depot must have been listening in to my garden-design dreams because it’s not even Thanksgiving yet and a heap of my favorite evergreen shrubs just had their prices slashed in an early Black Friday plant sale. And frankly, the prices were pretty decent even before they went on sale.

Let’s skip straight to the good bit, shall we?

While most boxwood shrubs grow incredibly slowly, sprinter boxwood lives up to its name, meaning you can buy a smaller, cheaper plant. And don’t worry that Buxus microphylla will grow too big because it maxes out at 2-4 feet high and wide: large enough to have an impact in your yard without taking over. Sprinter boxwood keeps its glossy green foliage year-round and has excellent resistance to diseases and pests, including boxwood blight. Suitable for zones 4-9, this handsome shrub is easily shaped to create structural evergreen mounds in a border, a low square hedge or appealing spheres in planters.

Thuja occidentalis ‘Anna van Vloten’ is a dwarf evergreen that naturally grows in a compact sphere without ever needing to be clipped. With wonderfully textural fan-like foliage, it keeps a bright golden-green tone year-round and grows well in zones 3-8. Anna’s Magic Ball arborvitae only grows to 10-15 inches high and wide and looks delightful dotted through a border. If you’re looking for compact shrubs to boost your curb appeal or want to add some stylish year-round planters to your patio, here’s the easy solution.

Here’s another dwarf cultivar of Thuja occidentalis that naturally grows in a compact ball shape without requiring any pruning. Danica America arborvitae is a little bigger at 2 feet high and wide and a brighter green, but what really sets it apart is its fan-like foliage that grows in vertical layers. The evergreen foliage is denser than Anna’s Magic Ball, too. Use it to create a smart geometric accent alongside a path or add stylish structure to a border without taking up too much space. It's one of the best evergreens for containers, too, and suitable for zones 3-7.

For instant style in zones 6-9, few evergreen shrubs have the striking aplomb of sky pencil holly. It’s a cultivar of the lovely Japanese holly and while it grows 6-10 feet tall, it stays a slender 1-2 feet wide with unusual vertical branches. The leaves are small, glossy and dark green – more like a boxwood than a holly – so the growth is dense, accentuating the shape. So, while sky pencil holly doesn’t boast red berries (though it does grow small black berries in fall), its silhouette provides more than enough drama. Happy in a large planter or in well-drained ground, sky pencil holly looks fabulous either side of a doorway or gate, or planted in a loose line, and is one of the best shrubs for a front yard.

So far, so green. And while it’s wonderful to have shrubs that bring texture and a year-round skeleton of leaves, some evergreen shrubs also deliver a generous splash of color. And Encore azalea is one of the very best flowering plants to add to your garden in fall. While many azaleas are deciduous, and older varieties only flower for a few short weeks in spring, the Encore series not only keeps its leaves through winter but repeat-blooms all through spring, summer and autumn. It maintains a tidy, rounded shape so requires very little pruning, and there are all sorts of flower colors to choose from. Suitable for zones 6-10, Autumn Royalty has bright magenta blooms and you’ll also find Autumn Lily with white flowers, Autumn Carnation with pink flowers, and Autumn Embers with red-orange flowers in Home Depot’s sale.

Euonymus fortunei ‘Roemertwo’ is one of those easy wins that every garden needs, requiring little looking after but working hard four seasons of the year. Don't be put off by the fact it's a wintercreeper as this cultivar is a compact mounding shrub. Its evergreen foliage doesn’t lose its variegation and revert to green like many shrubs, and thank goodness because the lime-green leaves have lovely gold margins that positively glow on a dark winter day. Adding to the color, Gold Splash wintercreeper boasts yellow fruit that open to reveal orange seeds in fall. Highly resistant to disease, this neat, ultra-tough shrub reaches 18-24 inches high and wide in zones 5-8.

Okay, so Viburnum nudum ‘Brandywine’ isn’t evergreen but it does look good all through winter on account of the multi-colored berries that cling to the branches months after leaves have fallen. Brandywine viburnum is one of the best berry-bearing shrubs to feel birds through winter as its berries only sweeten once the worst winter weather sets in, providing a valuable late-season pantry for our feathered friends. Those berries provide quite a show, too, starting green then shifting through pink and blue to a glossy dark purple. Hardy in zones 5-9, this low-maintenance shrub reaches 5-6 feet high.

Peace lilies may be entering a slower growth phase, but a few quick checks can make or break the healthy and vitality of your favorite houseplants over winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Your peace lily (Spathiphyllum) may well have spent the early part of fall thriving in its regular corner with little more than a weekly drink. But this can all change sharply when November arrives. Suddenly, the lower leaves droop, that trademark glossy sheen can look dull, and the leaf tips might turn dry and brown, even if you haven't changed your routine. The real shift is taking place in the house around the plant, and that’s easy to miss when the plant hasn’t moved an inch.

Peace lilies are naturally resilient, but they are sensitive to environmental shifts. The days are shorter, the sunlight angles have dropped, and central heating systems are kicking into gear. Good peace lily care through winter is largely about keeping up with those changes. The good news is that the fixes are small. It’s just about recognizing that your plant’s needs change as winter starts to set in.

By tweaking your habits and pausing unnecessary chores that may have been essential just a month earlier, you can protect root health and ensure your peace lily remains a centerpiece of lush green calm throughout these next few chilly months. Not only will these adjustments protect your favorite houseplant in winter, they will help to set the stage for more striking white spathes come spring. So here’s how to keep your peace lily healthy once the heat comes on…

Indoor winter living often creates conditions that clash with tropical houseplant health. We seal our doors, turn up the furnace, and seek out cozy, dry warmth. For a peace lily, that same forced-air heating strips ambient room humidity down to single digits while leaving drafty windowpanes ice-cold. Coexisting happily indoors through winter means balancing these conditions, providing the warmth your peace lily needs while protecting it against parched air, dark corners, and soggy soil.

Diagnosing leaf symptoms early in November prevents minor seasonal stress from escalating into root damage. If your entire plant suddenly collapses into a limp heap, check the soil before reaching for the watering can. If the potting mix is bone dry, a thorough drink will perk the foliage up within hours. If the mix feels soggy and heavy while the leaves hang limp, waterlogged roots are suffocating: stop watering now!

Brown, crispy leaf tips usually stem from low humidity, uneven moisture, or mineral salt accumulation from tap water. Occasional yellowing on a leaf lower down is normal ageing. However, multiple yellow leaves can indicate insufficient light or waterlogged compost or insufficient light. A long-probe soil moisture meter can help you determine deeper root moisture. I’m a big fan of the XLUX Long Probe Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, which delivers instant readings, so you can address overwatering and soggy potting mix before fungal rot sets in.

As for flowers, don't expect too many right now. Winter usually isn't when peace lilies bloom. A plant that rarely flowers at all, though, probably needs a brighter spot, unless it's still young (under a year old, some won't bloom yet). Knowing some of the warning signs, hopefully the following tasks will help you avoid calamity this winter…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The quickest way to harm a peace lily in November is sticking to a rigid summer watering schedule. As natural day length shortens and light intensity wanes, your plant enters a semi-dormant rest period. Transpiration slows, cell division halts, and roots need less moisture from the soil. A potting blend that dried out in 5 days during July can easily stay damp for 3 weeks in November. Keeping the soil constantly saturated starves roots of oxygen, eventually leading to Pythium root rot.

This step is easy: insert a finger a couple of inches (5cm) into the potting mix. Water only when it feels dry and crumbly to the touch. When you do water your peace lily, soak the root ball thoroughly with room-temperature water until it drains freely from the base, then empty any runoff collected in the saucer. Never leave a peace lily sitting in stagnant, chilled water. If your plant droops, check soil dampness first.

A nifty way of reducing the risks associated with poor drainage is to give your plants some elevation in the drainage tray. Kakuna Plant Pot Feet, available from Amazon, can be inserted between the pot and tray to minimize chills and waterlogging.

Peace lilies have an enduring reputation as indestructible low-light houseplants, but there is a difference between surviving and thriving. While they tolerate the subdued light of a shaded summer room, the dramatic drop in November’s daylight hours and sun intensity can throw low-light corners into near-darkness. Without help, your peace lily cannot produce the energy needed to support its broad leaf surface, leading to faded foliage, drooping stems, and a halt in flower spathe production.

Take time now to reassess where your peace lily sits and check how much light reaches the plant around noon. If needed, move the plant closer to an east or north-facing window, where it can absorb hours of bright, indirect winter daylight. Keep the leaves a few inches (8-10cm) back from direct contact with windowpanes, as freezing outdoor temperatures radiate through cold glass and will chill leaf tissue.

If placing your plant near a south or west-facing window where bright afternoon sun beams through, hang a sheer curtain to diffuse the rays; direct, unfiltered sunlight can still scorch foliage even in winter. For darker rooms lacking bright exposures, supplemental artificial light provides an easy fix. The GE BR30 Grow LED Light Bulb from Walmart fits a standard socket and lamp fixture, emitting balanced, warm-toned full-spectrum light that sustains photosynthesis through dark winter months.

Indoor central heating is a double hazard for peace lilies: it strips moisture from the air, while creating extreme temperature pockets. Peace lilies thrive in relative humidity levels between 50% and 60%. When heating systems get switched on, indoor humidity frequently plunges below 20%. This dry air saps moisture from leaf margins, causing crispy brown edges and papery tips. Position your plant away from forced-air vents, radiators, space heaters, and wood stoves. The blast of hot air will quickly scorch foliage. At the same time, keep plants shielded from exterior door drafts and chilly single-pane windows, maintaining a range of 65-80°F (18-27°C).

Skip leaf misting, which provides only a brief humidity spike and can encourage fungal leaf spotting. Instead, place your pot on a wide tray filled with pebbles and water (keeping the pot base resting above the water line). Alternatively, group multiple houseplants together, or run a small ultrasonic room humidifier nearby. To help you track things, buy a digital sensor like the TempPro TP50 Digital Room Temperature and Humidity Monitor, available from The Home Depot. This compact digital sensor monitors relative humidity and ambient temperature fluctuations, helping you pinpoint cold drafts and heating hotspots.

During the dark days of late fall and winter, feeding a peace lily does far more harm than good. Because diminished daylight slows metabolic activity, the plant is not producing new tissue or developing roots. Adding liquid houseplant fertilizer during this semi-dormant time means mineral salts can build up in the potting soil. Over several weeks, this salt buildup can burn roots and brown leaf tips. Now is the time to withhold all supplemental feeding until active spring growth returns in late March.

Similarly, postpone repotting until the warmer, brighter days of spring. It doesn’t matter if you see a few roots poking out of the drainage holes: peace lilies tolerate being slightly pot-bound and recover faster in spring. Moving a sluggish plant into a larger pot now can shock them. The only exception is emergency repotting. If a plant has collapsed from severe root rot, gently tip it from its pot and rinse away old soil. Trim off brown mushy roots with sterile shears, and repot into fresh, well-aerated potting mix. A great lightweight blend for emergency winter repotting is Espoma Organic Houseplant Potting Soil Mix, available at The Home Depot.

In just a few weeks, broad peace lily leaves collect a fine film of household dust, pet dander, and airborne grease. Dusty foliage can be severely limiting in winter. Dust acts as a barrier, scattering what little winter light reaches the leaves and reducing the plant's already limited photosynthetic capacity. Cleaning the foliage is a quick, high-reward task that keeps leaves breathing and photosynthesizing efficiently. Support each leaf from beneath with one hand, and gently wipe the upper and lower surfaces with a soft cloth moistened with room-temperature water.

As you clean, inspect the leaf undersides and stem junctions for pests. Dry winter heating can encourage rapid outbreaks unless you catch them early. Bits of white fluff could be citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Flat tan bumps are often brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum). Faint speckling and webbing usually mean twospotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), which thrive in dry, heated rooms. Gently dab mealybug clusters with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, or treat leaf undersides with a gentle organic insecticidal soap or neem oil wash. Bonide Captain Jack’s Neem Oil Spray, available from Amazon, is a brilliant organic way of controlling spider mites, scale, and mealybugs.

By giving your peace lily a little focused attention in November, you provide the support it needs to navigate the winter months with ease. Dialing back the watering can, finding a brighter pocket of filtered daylight, raising ambient moisture levels, and letting the roots rest will keep the foliage healthy and glossy.

Set up well in November, a peace lily usually comes through winter looking much like it did in summer, just growing a little slower. The fertilizer and the bigger pot can wait until spring, and so can you. When longer spring days return, your well-rested peace lily will be primed to surge back into active growth, rewarding you with fresh green leaves and a striking display of signature white blooms.

#7966. Justice Department Announces Coordinated Actions to Combat North Korean Remote IT Worker Schemes Affecting More Than 70 U.S. Companies

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today the Department of Justice announced coordinated actions against the Democratic People’s Republic of North Korea (DPRK) government’s schemes to fund its regime through remote information technology (IT) work for U.S. companies. These actions include an indictment, two arrests, searches of multiple known or suspected “laptop farms” in Texas pursuant to “Operation Lonestar Roundup,” and the seizure of approximately 187 computer devices used by DPRK IT workers.

“North Korea’s rogue regime uses its pervasive IT worker schemes to raise revenue for various illicit purposes, including the development of weapons that could ultimately target the United States or its allies,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “These schemes threaten the security of the IT systems and data of the deceived U.S. employers and leave countless victims of identity theft. NSD, along with our law enforcement partners, will use every available tool to track down anyone assisting the DPRK and to protect our national security.”

“Threats posed by nation-states like North Korea are a stark reminder that our adversaries will go to great measures to exploit our nation’s economic strength to further and fuel their own nefarious agendas,” said U.S. Attorney David M. Toepfer for the Northern District of Ohio. “We are thankful to FBI Cleveland for their incredible work and persistence to put a stop to these bad actors. These charges serve as an urgent alert to all U.S. companies to remain vigilant in their hiring practices.”

“This investigation is about far more than fraud,” said U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould for the Northern District of Texas. “It is about a hostile foreign regime infiltrating American companies through stolen identities and covert access points inside our own borders. Every laptop farm we dismantle shuts down a revenue stream that the North Korean government relies on to fund weapons programs that threaten global stability. Operation Lonestar Roundup sends a clear message: we will not allow enemies of the United States to exploit our businesses or compromise our national security.”

“North Korea continues to deploy remote IT workers using stolen identities to infiltrate American companies and generate revenue for the regime and its weapons programs,” said Assistant Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Division. “Today, the FBI and DOJ announced a series of coordinated actions against this threat, securing charges against 14 individuals, conducting two arrests, seizing nearly 190 devices, and executing operations at more than 40 suspected ‘laptop farms’ across Texas. Close coordination between the private sector and federal law enforcement was central to this operation. To further combat the threat, the FBI has issued a Public Service Announcement with detailed mitigation guidance for U.S. companies.”

Sun Sheng Ming, et al. Indictment and Arrests – Northern District of Ohio

Today, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced the arrests of U.S. nationals Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas pursuant to a four-count wire fraud, money laundering, and identity theft indictment. The indictment describes a multi-year fraud scheme by Bostelle, Pena, and their co-conspirators to obtain remote IT work with U.S. companies that generated more than $3 million in revenue. The indictment also charges China-based Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang, Jin Long for their roles in the scheme. The identities of two additional defendants remain under seal.

According to the indictment, from 2019 to in or around July 2025, DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure to appear as though they were U.S. persons working from within the United States. They also relied on U.S.-based facilitators who received and hosted multiple laptop computers — issued by victim U.S. companies — at their residences in the United States (“laptop farms”), housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts.

In total, the scheme impacted more than 70 U.S. company employers and generated approximately $3 million in revenue for IT workers. The revenue is believed to have been sent to sanctioned entities controlled by the DPRK. Victim employers included companies in the health care, communications, cyber support, retail, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio, sixteen additional states, and the District of Columbia.

The FBI Cleveland Field Office is investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Duncan T. Brown for the Northern District of Ohio and Trial Attorney Neeraj Gupta of the National Security Division’s National Security Cyber Section are prosecuting the case.

Operation Lonestar Roundup Disrupts Multiple Known or Suspected Laptop Farms in Texas

Between Sept. 21 and Sept. 25, the FBI conducted searches and other law enforcement action at over 40 residences in Texas known to be, or suspected of operating as, laptop farms for DPRK IT workers. Over the course of the entire operation (Operation Lonestar Roundup), the FBI seized approximately 187 laptops and KVM (keyboard, video, mouse) devices that DPRK IT workers and their U.S.-based facilitators used to commit fraud, obtain remote employment, and generate revenue for the North Korean regime’s sanctioned weapons programs. U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has identified this group of DPRK IT workers and their helpers as “Famous Chollima.”

Investigators discovered that the DPRK operatives allegedly used a network of fraudulent email accounts to facilitate their criminal activity. The following accounts were among those identified as being used in these schemes:

Employers are encouraged to add these accounts to the list of indicators they use to identify and disrupt DPRK IT worker employment.

Today, the FBI published a public service announcement describing the evolving DPRK IT worker threat, including tips on how to detect the threat. Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals. Additionally, CrowdStrike today published a blog post describing its efforts at monitoring customer networks for DPRK IT worker activity and its successful collaboration with the FBI to disrupt this threat.

The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas, the FBI’s Dallas Field Office, and the FBI’s Cyber Division coordinated Operation Lonestar Roundup. Valuable assistance was provided by the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio.

Today’s announcements represent the Department’s latest actions to combat North Korean IT worker schemes as part of a joint NSD and FBI Cyber and Counterintelligence Divisions effort, the DPRK RevGen: Domestic Enabler Initiative. This effort prioritizes targeting and disrupting the DPRK’s illicit revenue generation schemes and its U.S.-based enablers. The Department previously announced other actions pursuant to the initiative, including in June 2025, November 2025, April 2026, and May 2026.

As described in Public Service Announcements published in May 2024, January 2025, July 2025, and today, North Korean remote IT workers posing as legitimate remote IT workers have committed data extortion and exfiltrated the proprietary and sensitive data from U.S. companies. DPRK IT worker schemes typically involve the use of stolen identities, alias emails, social media, online cross-border payment platforms, and online job site accounts, as well as false websites, proxy computers, and witting and unwitting third parties located in the U.S. and elsewhere. North Korean IT workers leverage these third parties, which include U.S.-based individuals, to gain fraudulent employment and access to U.S. company networks to generate this revenue.

Other public advisories about the threats, red flag indicators, and potential mitigation measures for these schemes include a May 2022 advisory released by the FBI, Department of the Treasury, and Department of State; a July 2023 advisory from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and guidance issued in October 2023 by the United States and the Republic of Korea (South Korea). As described the May 2022 advisory, North Korean IT workers have been known individually to earn up to $300,000 annually, generating hundreds of millions of dollars collectively each year, on behalf of designated entities, such as the North Korean Ministry of Defense and others directly involved in the DPRK’s weapons programs.

The U.S. Department of State has offered potential rewards for up to $5 million in support of international efforts to disrupt the DPRK’s illicit financial activities, including for cybercrimes, money laundering, and sanctions evasion.

The details in the above-described court documents are merely allegations. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

Your empty tomato cages can shelter tender shrubs from frost and snow all winter and help safeguard next summer's flowers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wrapped in frost cloth or burlap, an old tomato cage becomes a cheap but effective shelter to protect plants this winter. All sorts of tender shrubs and perennials need winter protection, and temporarily shielding even hardy plants from the worst of the weather can help them thrive. So if you're about to pack away your tomato cages in the shed, stop – they've got another job to do now it's time to winterize garden plants this fall.

Pulling up tomato plants and stacking their cages in the shed until spring is one of the last big gardening jobs of the season. That's a lot of good wire sitting around in the dark all winter, and this trick puts it right back to work. Most gardens have a plant or two that struggles through the cold months, and overwintering plants usually means spending money on shrub covers, frost tents or frames, or insulating zip-up plant jackets built for the job. None of it costs much alone, but the outlay adds up across a whole bed and your old cage can do much of that same work to winterize plants.

This trick won't save everything, but for the right plants a tomato cage wrapped in frost cloth or burlap is a smart, cheap way to help your garden get through winter unscathed. So, if you're gardening on a budget and wondering how to protect plants in winter, here's the smart solution.

Throw insulating fabric straight over a shrub and it settles right onto the leaves and buds, and cold will seep through wherever it touches. Wet snow is worse. Its weight can bend or snap branches under the cover. But put a tomato cage in there first and the fabric sits on the frame instead, with a little gap between cover and plant. This method also gives you a frame to fasten the fabric to so it stays put when the wind picks up.

Start with the cage itself. You'll probably find dried leaves and sections of vine still wound through the wire. If last summer's plants had Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) or early blight (Alternaria solani), those scraps can carry it over, so pull every one out and disinfect by scrubbing the cage with diluted household bleach and a rinse.

Next comes the fit. Lower the clean cage over the plant and see where the branches end up. Any branch poking through the wire is, more or less, where the fabric will touch the plant later, so the stems need room inside. Push the legs down firmly and, out in an open, windy bed, tie it to a sturdy stake if needs be.

Now wrap the frame in breathable frost cloth or horticultural fleece: one Agfabric frost blanket, available from Home Depot, covers more than one cage. Fasten the fabric to the frame using clips like these stainless steel garden clips from Walmart. Take the fabric right down to the soil as warmth comes up out of the ground at night and a gap at the bottom lets it leak out. Pin the fabric to the ground with galvanized landscape staples like these from Walmart.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Skip plastic wrap, because the plant needs to breathe and a wrapped cage heats up fast on mild afternoons and damp, still air favors gray mold (Botrytis cinerea). Even without a waterproof wrap, peek underneath every few days and let some fresh air in if needs be. Once the cold snap is over, take the temporary covers off, leaving the frame in place ready for the next weather dip.

Depending on your USDA zone, the plants that need winterizing in fall aren't just those that aren't hardy enough to survive plummeting temperatures: you can use this trick to extend a crop or protect next year's flower show, too. Ever had a hydrangea leaf out nicely and then barely bloom? Bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) is the classic candidate because it forms next year's flower buds on old wood, and those buds sit on bare stems all winter. Hard freezes can kill these delicate buds so while the foliage comes through just fine the following year, blooms are few and far between.

Hybrid tea roses and perennials that are borderline hardy in your zone are good candidates too. If you've planted young shrubs this year – especially if you've been tempted by Black Friday sales on evergreen shrubs and you're planting late in fall – they'll also benefit from being kept cozy during cold snaps. Boxwood and other small evergreens can pick up winter burn from drying wind and sun, and burlap like this Wellco natural burlap roll at Home Depotcuts down on both without pressing on the foliage.

Of course, you'll need to match the plant to the cage size. But if you're planning to upgrade your tomato cages to use a more substantial modular tomato support set-up like these heavy-duty square tomato cages, also from Home Depot anyway, it makes sense to do so now when you can use them to protect bigger shrubs that need a wider frame.

Once the plant goes dormant, usually after several hard frosts, a sturdy cage can be packed with loose insulation to provide further insulation too. Dry shredded leaves, straw or pine straw like this from Amazon is best. On a bigleaf hydrangea, you can fill right up around the buds, while roses mostly need the extra insulation over the crown and lower canes.

Keep that fill dry and loose. Leaves raked off a wet lawn and packed tight against living foliage or a crown stay soggy, and that can lead to rot, so let them dry out first before covering with frost fabric. In spring, pull out the fill a little at a time once the worst cold has passed.

Frost cloth doesn't make any heat of its own, but only slows the loss of warmth rising from the ground at night, buying a few degrees on a clear, still night. In a long, deep freeze, the soil underneath cools off too, and that leaves the cover less and less to work with. Truly tropical plants won't turn winter-hardy inside a wrapped cage, either: hibiscus and mandevilla belong indoors once nights turn chilly, well ahead of frost. In colder regions, some tender plants on the edge of hardiness still do better potted up and stored in a frost-free spot.

For most of the year, a tomato cage has one job. But with a cozy comforter of frost cloth, a few clips and a bit of care, this garden staple picks up a second role in winter, sheltering plants that would otherwise need a store-bought cover and helping to ensure another flower-filled year in your garden. When spring comes, unwrap your precious plant, hose off the cage and send it back to the tomato bed. It's the same old cage pulling double duty, and this trick to reuse it over winter barely costs a dime.

#7963. ‘Fireworks’ Goldenrod: A Pollinator Favorite with Bold Yellow Blooms

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Learn more about ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod, one of Melissa Starkey’s favorite underappreciated native plants.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

We’re moving into fall for this next pick. Goldenrods are amazing plants in general, even though they get a bad rap. People sometimes associate them with allergies, but they are confusing goldenrod with ragweed (Ambrosia spp.). Not all goldenrods are too aggressive. They are host plants for over 120 different moth and butterfly caterpillars, and the seeds feed birds and other animals.

If I had to pick just one to highlight, ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod would be my gateway plant to goldenrods. Anyone can use it in their garden, including in formal settings and in containers. ‘Fireworks’ is an appropriate name for this cultivar, as spires of bright yellow flowers explode in early to mid-autumn. It has a compact, clumping habit. This goldenrod can spread a little bit in moist soil, but it is not difficult to control, and it will stay put if you site it in a drier area. It likes full sun, but I have it in partial shade and it still looks lovely.

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.

Goldenrod photo courtesy of Deborah Gruca.

#7962. No Problem with Recognizing Islamic Talaq Divorce from Dubai, When Wife Didn't Want to Stay Married

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Schultz v. Stevenson, decided today by California Court of Appeal Judges Peter Krause, Shama Hakim Mesiwala, and Stacy Boulware Eurie:

In 2004, [the parties] purchased a residential property in Grass Valley, California, taking title as "husband and wife as joint tenants." In 2020, [husband] Schultz obtained a judgment of divorce from [wife] Stevenson in Dubai, United Arab Emirates (UAE). The Dubai divorce decree addressed marital status and child custody only; it made no findings related to division of property or spousal support.

Years later, Schultz commenced an action … to partition the Grass Valley property [by ordering it sold and the proceeds split -EV]. Stevenson opposed partition, arguing that the Dubai divorce decree is not enforceable in California and therefore the property is community property and not subject to partition [since California law does not allow partition of community property among married parties -EV]. The trial court ultimately … [decided] in favor of Schultz, finding that the parties are divorced and that the property is not community property….

Stevenson … argues that the trial court abused its discretion by extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree because it was based on Islamic (Sharia) laws that violate state public policy and constitutional principles of equal protection and due process…. [S]he argues that the Dubai divorce is not entitled to comity because it is based on a talaq pronouncement of divorce, which violates California's public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment. [Generally, a talaq divorce can only be initiated by a husband. -EV] Stevenson contends therefore that she and Schultz are still married, and that the Nevada County property is community property, which is not subject to partition.

We conclude that Stevenson has failed to show that the trial court erred in extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree.

Under the doctrine of comity, courts of this nation generally will give effect to the judgment of a foreign nation if the foreign court had proper jurisdiction and enforcement of the judgment will not prejudice the rights of United States citizens or violate domestic public policy…. Even if we agree that parts of Sharia law—such as a talaq pronouncement of divorce—are contrary to domestic public policy favoring gender equality and constitutional protections against gender-based disparate treatment, the mere fact that some laws of the foreign nation are inconsistent with those of the sovereign does not preclude application of comity.

The basic principle of judicial comity is that "'a court should not assume to disturb another court's disposition of a controversy unless there are good reasons for doing so.'" The standard for refusing to enforce a foreign judgment on public policy grounds is high and infrequently met. The standard "'is not simply that the law is contrary to our public policy, but that it is so offensive to our public policy as to be "'prejudicial to recognized standards of morality and to the general interests of the citizens….'"' [E]ven when a foreign law offends public policy, 'it may still be applied in a limited context where the potential harm is minimal….'" (See In re Dalip Singh Bir's Estate (Cal. App. 1948) [in context of intestate succession, foreign law permitting polygamy may be applied under principles of comity].)

Here, we are not persuaded that extending comity to the Dubai divorce decree impermissibly prejudiced Stevenson's rights or flouted state public policy favoring gender equality. It is important to remember that the Dubai judgment only adjudicated two issues—marital status and child custody—and that the trial court extended comity to the judgment as it related to the status of marriage only. {Stevenson contends that issues related to child custody and support have been rendered moot as the children have reached the age of majority.} Since Stevenson plainly did not wish to remain married to Schultz, we cannot say that it was an abuse of discretion for the trial court to recognize the Dubai judgment as dissolving marital status.

The premise underlying Stevenson's claim of prejudice appears to be that recognizing the foreign divorce precludes her from obtaining spousal support and an equitable division of the marital property. We disagree with this premise…. As noted, the Dubai judgment only adjudicated the issues of marital status and child custody. It did not address, and therefore has no effect upon, spousal support or the division of community property in California….

In reaching this conclusion, we note that the trial court has ordered the partition and sale of property but has not yet determined how the proceeds will be disbursed, reserving jurisdiction "to order the manner in which the sale proceeds are to be disbursed, and to order equitable adjustments that the Court considers just and appropriate." It is therefore premature for us to consider whether the distribution of proceeds amounts to an abuse of discretion….

Robin D. Shofner (Scale LLP) represents Schultz.

NEXT: "The 'Birds Aren't Real' Guy Was Just a Little Ahead of the Curve"

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. In four months, the violent crime initiative also seized enough fentanyl to kill 52 million people

The FBI and its law enforcement partners are announcing the results of Summer Heat 2.0, a four-month violent crime initiative that resulted in 8,927 arrests, the seizure of deadly fentanyl and cocaine, and 5,013 dangerous illegally possessed weapons taken off American streets.

“This year’s Summer Heat was our second straight nationwide offensive to crush violent crime all over the country, and the results were outstanding,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Even after last year’s unprecedented numbers, all 56 FBI field offices stepped up and delivered even higher numbers this year—arresting almost 9,000 subjects, up 3% from Summer Heat last year; seizing 63% more fentanyl; identifying or locating 1,410 children, 34% higher than last year; and recovering over 5,000 weapons, up 120% from 2025. Major cities across America saw increases as high as 80% in arrests compared to last summer alone. When this FBI elevated ‘crushing violent crime’ to one of our top priorities, we moved 2,000 FBI personnel out of Washington and permanently into the field—making the decisive call to go on offense. This FBI isn’t waiting for violent criminals, drug traffickers, and weapons dealers to devastate our communities any longer. As a result, under the Trump administration’s leadership, we have achieved the most prolific reduction in violent crime in U.S. history.”  Between June 1 and September 20, the FBI and its 56 field offices surged resources alongside state and local partners to execute federal warrants on violent criminals and fugitives, dismantle violent gangs and transnational criminal organizations, identify and rescue child victims, and resolve violent crime cases in Indian Country.

The FBI’s Summer Heat 2.0 initiative achieved additional victories with 687 kilograms of fentanyl seized: an amount equal to 52 million lethal doses. Of the 8,927 arrests, more than 5,900 arrests fell under the FBI’s violent crime and gang program.

A Homeland Security Task Force (HSTF) takedown across two states, Operation Turf War, kicked off the FBI’s 2026 Summer Heat initiative. FBI Pittsburgh, in coordination with West Virginia’s HSTF, netted 32 narcotics and weapons-related arrests. In a separate effort in July 2026, FBI Los Angeles executed 17 federal arrest warrants and 49 search warrants in connection with Operation Hard Ball. The operation united FBI Los Angeles with law enforcement from Canada and Europe to investigate an organized crime group accused of a litany of criminal acts. And in yet another example of the success of Operation Summer Heat, FBI San Juan and its partners led Operation Taking Back West, which resulted in the indictment of 81 members of a violent criminal gang.   The FBI first launched the Summer Heat initiative for three months in 2025 to deploy a multi-pronged offensive to crush violent crime. The announcement of Operation Summer Heat 2.0 results follows on the heels of historic drops in crime across the U.S., according to the FBI’s 2025 UCR Summary of Reported Crimes in the Nation.
